item.title: Human and AI Judgment in EFL Speaking Assessment: Psychometric Dependability, Feedback Quantity and Coverage, and Exploratory Teacher Perspectives
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
This study examined human-AI judgment in EFL speaking assessment as a measurement problem relevant to research on individual differences: how consistently do expert raters and repeated AI sessions preserve between-person differences in a complex performance? Thirty oral-performance samples from first-year Chinese university English majors were evaluated by four experienced EFL teachers and by ChatGPT-4o across four repeated sessions using the same holistic and accuracy-fluency-complexity framework. Score distributions were summarized descriptively; human-rater intraclass correlations and generalizability-theory G- and D-studies evaluated dependability. Feedback quantity and thematic coverage were summarized descriptively, and post-results interviews with the same four teacher-raters were analyzed as exploratory participant reflections. Teachers produced more dependable single ratings. Holistic phi coefficients were 0.54 for one ChatGPT-4o session and 0.65 for one teacher, increasing to 0.83 and 0.88 with four assessments. Analytic single-assessment coefficients ranged from 0.54 to 0.56 for ChatGPT-4o and 0.61 to 0.65 for teachers. Across holistic and analytic scoring, a phi coefficient of at least 0.80 was reached with four repeated ChatGPT-4o sessions but three independent teachers. ChatGPT-4o’s analytic dimensions showed limited differentiation from its holistic scoring: accuracy matched the holistic score in all 120 AI ratings, while fluency and complexity differed in only three and four ratings, respectively. ChatGPT-4o also produced more rubric-relevant comments descriptively, while the four teacher-raters emphasized human oversight for contextual and interpersonal interpretation. The study contributes to intelligence research at the level of psychometric measurement and human-AI judgment: assessor systems can differentially preserve observed individual differences in complex performance. EFL speaking was not treated as an intelligence test, and unmeasured cognitive mechanisms were not inferred from the score patterns.

item.title: Generative AI use and scientific literacy among 15-year-olds in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China: the mediating role of academic help-seeking
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading and self-regulated learning, we examined whether GenAI use for schoolwork is related to scientific literacy directly and through two components of self-regulated learning, academic help-seeking and metacognitive strategy use, and whether the purpose of use matters. Methods We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment 2025 (PISA 2025) data from 12,191 15-year-old students in 374 schools in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China. Weighted two-level mediation models compared students within the same school, used all ten plausible values, and evaluated indirect effects with Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Results were checked against a design-based model with school fixed effects and balanced repeated replication weights. Results Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates reported more help-seeking ( β = 0.17) and more metacognitive strategy use ( β = 0.30). Help-seeking was positively associated with scientific literacy, yielding a positive indirect effect ( β = 0.013, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]); the indirect effect through metacognitive strategies was smaller ( β = 0.007) and was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. The direct association between GenAI use and scientific literacy was negative ( β = −0.048, about 4 PISA points), and the positive indirect effects offset about 40% of it, leaving a small negative total association ( β = −0.028). Purpose mattered: among users, using GenAI “to help me learn” was associated with higher scientific literacy (+5.8 points per response category), whereas using it to summarize texts, research new topics, or draft assignments was associated with lower scores (−6.6 points). The results did not differ by gender or socioeconomic status and were identical under the design-based model. Discussion GenAI use for schoolwork is associated with scientific literacy through opposing pathways: a positive one through academic help-seeking and a negative direct one, and the direction of the association differs by purpose of use. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations may partly reflect which students use GenAI rather than the effects of its use.

item.title: The relationship between attitudes toward artificial intelligence and digital literacy skills: a sports sciences perspective
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported applications in sports sciences, such as performance analysis, injury risk prediction, and data-driven training, underscores the importance of understanding the link between students’ digital competencies and their perceptions of AI. This study examined the relationship between sports science students’ attitudes toward AI and their levels of digital literacy. Methods A correlational survey design was used. The sample consisted of 229 female and 314 male undergraduate students ( n = 543; Mage = 21.16, SD = 4.5) from 13 state and foundation universities across Türkiye. Data were collected through a demographic information form, the Digital Literacy Scale, and the General Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 25, JASP 0.19.3.0, AMOS 24, and Minitab 20. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were used to test the relationships among variables. Results Positive attitudes toward AI were significantly and positively associated with digital literacy ( β = 0.55, p < 0.001), whereas negative attitudes showed a weaker but significant negative association ( β = −0.20, p < 0.001). The model explained 38.4% of the variance in digital literacy ( R 2 = 0.384). Discussion These results suggest that positive AI perceptions may support students’ engagement with digital environments, whereas negative perceptions may constrain it. The study emphasizes the importance of educational experiences that enhance AI awareness and strengthen digital literacy within sports science programs.

item.title: Label or not: AI-generated news labels and perceived credibility among Chinese readers
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence increasingly writes the news, and Chinese regulation has required explicit labels on AI-generated content since September 2025, yet what such labels do to readers’ trust remains an open question. This experiment tested whether an AI-generated news label changes perceived credibility, whether perceived human involvement explains the change, and whether readers’ AI literacy conditions it. Methods A sample of 1,024 Chinese adults (51.7% female; mean age 30.8 years) recruited through an online panel was randomly assigned to read one of two news stories that either carried a prominent AI-generated label or carried no authorship label, in a 2 (label: AI-generated vs. no label) × 2 (news topic: health technology vs. urban culture) between-subjects design with 256 per cell. Participants rated perceived human involvement, message credibility, and their own AI literacy. Results The label lowered perceived credibility (β = −0.31, p < 0.001) and perceived human involvement ( F (1, 1,020) = 218.60, p < 0.001). Involvement mediated the label effect on credibility: the indirect effect was β = −0.19, 95% CI [−0.23, −0.16], about three fifths of the total effect. AI literacy moderated the label-to-involvement path (β = 0.10, p < 0.001): the label penalty was β = −0.52 at low literacy and β = −0.32 at high literacy, and the index of moderated mediation was β = 0.05, 95% CI [0.02, 0.08]. Discussion The credibility cost of AI news labels travels through perceived human involvement and concentrates among readers with little AI literacy. Labeling regimes can keep AI-generated news transparent without flatlining trust, but they work best alongside AI literacy education.

item.title: Empirical study on how lower limb exoskeleton robots improve older adults’ physical performance through psychological mechanisms
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objective This study aims to explore how lower limb exoskeleton robots enhance physical performance in older adults and clarify the mediating role of psychological factors during human-robot interaction exercises. Methods The study focused on healthy older adults in the community and used a randomized controlled trial design along with qualitative research methods. A total of 60 participants aged 60–75 were selected and divided into an lower limb exoskeleton robots intervention group and a control group. Through an 8-week standardized exercise intervention, data on physiological performance indicators such as participants’ walking speed, stride length, gait variability coefficient, 6-min walking distance, and balance sway values, as well as psychological indicators such as perceived fatigue, exercise self-efficacy, and balance confidence, were collected. Qualitative research was also conducted, delving into the real psychological experiences and subjective perceptions of older adults using lower limb exoskeleton robots, and explaining the deeper mechanisms behind the quantitative results. Results After the intervention, the intervention group showed significant improvements in walking speed, stride length, and gait stability compared to the control group ( p < 0.05). Exercise self-efficacy and balance confidence significantly increased while perceived exertion significantly decreased ( p < 0.01). Mediation analysis indicated that exercise self-efficacy and perceived exertion served as a chain mediator between the use of lower limb exoskeleton robots and physical performance in older adults. Conclusion Lower limb exoskeleton robots can not only enhance physical abilities through mechanical support but also improve psychological perception and strengthen exercise confidence, creating a positive cycle of ‘device assistance—psychological empowerment—improved physical performance’. This provides new theoretical support and practical pathways for elderly rehabilitation and healthy aging interventions.

item.title: Perceived career impacts of artificial intelligence and career decision-making self-efficacy among Chinese college students: the mediating roles of career planning and career anxiety
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping labor market structures and transforming how college students perceive their future career development. Understanding the psychological processes associated with the relationships between perceptions of AI and career-related outcomes has therefore become increasingly important. Drawing on Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study examined the relationships between perceived career impacts of AI and career decision-making self-efficacy among college students, with particular attention to the indirect roles of career planning and career anxiety. A questionnaire survey was conducted with 415 Chinese college students, and the proposed hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling. The results showed that positive perceived career impacts of AI were positively associated with career decision-making self-efficacy, with career planning representing an indirect pathway in this relationship. In contrast, negative perceived career impacts of AI were not directly associated with career decision-making self-efficacy but were indirectly associated with lower self-efficacy through an indirect association involving career anxiety. These findings indicate that college students' perceptions of AI are associated with career decision-making self-efficacy through distinct cognitive and affective processes. The study provides empirical support for the applicability of SCCT in understanding career development in the context of AI and enriches the literature on the relationships between AI-related career perceptions and students' career decision-making processes.

item.title: Production cues and conditional reliance in AI-mediated news: a three-study investigation of audience judgment under information asymmetry
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into digital news presentation, understanding how audiences interpret AI-related production cues is critical to explaining evaluations of journalistic authority and reliance. Yet existing research has largely focused on transparency and generalized trust, leaving the relationships among production cues, perceived journalistic attributes, cognitive authority, and context-dependent reliance insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we propose a Signal–Attribute–Authority–Conditional Reliance (SAAC) framework and evaluate it across three complementary studies involving Chinese digital-news users: a 2 × 2 randomized experiment manipulating AI-disclosure and human editorial-review cues while holding the underlying AI-produced news stimulus constant ( n = 473); a cross-sectional survey integrating structural modeling, predictive analysis, and necessary condition analysis ( n = 522); and explanatory semi-structured interviews ( n = 29). The experiment showed that production cues influenced several post-exposure evaluations despite identical news content. Survey findings revealed associations linking perceived disclosure quality and human editorial oversight to perceived news quality and accountability, with further associations involving journalistic cognitive authority, conditional reliance, and acceptance intention, although explanatory and predictive performance remained modest. Interviews indicated that participants distinguished technological presentation capability from journalistic source qualification and evaluated reliance in relation to news topics, perceived stakes, editorial involvement, and institutional safeguards. Together, the findings suggest that,within the present study settings, AI-mediated news acceptance is better understood as an I nstitutionally situated and conditionally bounded judgment than as a simple function of transparency or generalized trust.

item.title: The relationship between AI-assisted learning and academic performance through learning engagement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has raised an important question regarding whether AI-assisted learning is associated with students' academic performance. Although prior studies have highlighted the potential benefits of AI in education, the psychological processes underlying this relationship remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the association between AI-assisted learning and academic performance, with a particular focus on the mediating role of learning engagement as an educational psychological mechanism. Methods Data were collected through an online survey of university students in Shanxi Province, China. Using a convenience and snowball sampling strategy, 438 valid responses were obtained and analyzed. The study employed multi-item scales to measure AI-assisted learning, learning engagement, and academic performance, including a literature-informed self-developed scale for AI-assisted learning and adapted scales for learning engagement and academic performance. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 27.0 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA) and AMOS 24.0 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA), including descriptive statistics, reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, structural equation modeling (SEM), and bootstrapped mediation analysis. Results and discussion The results indicate that AI-assisted learning is positively associated with both learning engagement and academic performance. Learning engagement also has a significant positive effect on academic performance. More importantly, the findings show that learning engagement partially mediates the relationship between AI-assisted learning and academic performance, highlighting the role of students' psychological involvement in the learning process. These findings suggest that the educational value of AI-assisted learning is associated not only with technological support but also with students' psychological engagement in learning activities. This study contributes to the literature on AI in education by providing a psychologically grounded explanation of the relationship between AI-assisted learning and academic outcomes. It also offers practical implications for educators and institutions seeking to integrate AI into higher education in ways that foster meaningful engagement and enhance effective learning.

item.title: Meditation as a bioactive intervention: evidence of translational potential via Connectivity Mapping and TMS neurophysiology
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Abstract Meditation practices are often used as non-pharmacological adjunct therapy for managing stress and well-being benefits. We propose that beneath their non-pharmacological facade, meditation practices might operate via drug target modulation having profound neurophysiological effects. Firstly, we leverage the Connectivity Map (CMap) to investigate (a) the overlap between meditation-induced molecular signatures and established drug responses, and (b) the pathways and mechanisms contributing to meditation’ potential therapeutic effects. This was studied in a comprehensive temporal RNAseq dataset comprising premeditation, meditation, and follow-up stages from a clinical trial involving 106 participants practising inner engineering meditation. Meditation signatures overlapped with over 438 drugs, but predominantly with drugs targeting the neuroactive ligand receptor pathways, capable of modulating the brain’s excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance. Next, to bridge the meditation-induced molecular changes to measurable neurophysiological effects, we performed a comprehensive meta-analysis of drugs affecting E/I balance through the lens of non-invasive brain stimulation, i.e., transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS-EMG and TMS-EEG). Using multiple correspondence analysis, we then clustered the CMap informed neuroactive drugs and their E/I effects on the same latent space. We found that meditation’s effects mimic drugs targeting the GABAergic, Glutametergic and other neuromodulatory system pathways. Our findings lead to a working model to objectively test neurophysiological changes resulting from meditation that can lead to evidence-based clinical applications. Overall, these findings support the view that meditation acts as a biologically active intervention capable of modulating molecular pathways and cortical excitability, rather than functioning solely as a psychological or contemplative practice.

item.title: Different Logics, Similar Intentions: Heterogeneity in How Employees Evaluate AI Adoption
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption at work has documented heterogeneity in user attitudes and adoption profiles, but less is known about whether employees differ in how they weight adoption-relevant information. In a within-subject structured-profile experiment, 446 employees provided 7,136 intention judgments across 16 profiles that varied AI adoption benefits, barriers, replacement vulnerability, and anticipated work harm. Multilevel regression mixture model analysis identified four latent decision-policy classes with different estimated weights on opportunity and threat cues; class mean intentions were not statistically distinguishable. Drawing on multiple-cue judgment theory, we interpret this pattern as heterogeneity in cue utilization rather than simply in attitude levels. Explaining and managing AI adoption therefore requires attention to latent decision policies, because aggregate effect estimates and profiles based on mean levels can conceal differences in cue responsiveness that shape how employees evaluate AI.

item.title: From Briefing to Prompt: How Users Translate Textual Design Instructions into Text-to-Image Prompts
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Text-to-image systems support creative, educational, and professional work, yet how users translate briefs into effective prompts remains underexplored. This study examines prompt formulation and refinement by 23 participants using ChatGPT with DALL·E 3 under two task configurations: low-detail briefings with multiple reformulations and high-detail briefings with one reformulation. A structured literature review and qualitative analysis of 81 prompts, 81 images, interviews, and observation notes, supported by inter-coder agreement, identified recurring strategies, difficulties expressing visual intentions, and refinement patterns. High-detail/single-reformulation tasks produced semantically denser prompts and closer alignment with intended outcomes; low-detail/multiple-reformulation tasks encouraged exploratory prompting and interpretive variation. Because briefing detail and reformulation opportunities varied together, these findings reflect task-configuration differences, not isolated effects of briefing complexity. Framing prompting as cognitive and creative mediation in human–AI interaction, the study proposes a process model spanning briefing interpretation, semantic extraction, visual attribute selection, prompt structuring, generation, and refinement, requiring further validation.

item.title: AI Is Not an Employee: Workplace Mental Models and the Context Discovery Gap in Human-AI Interaction
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
AI adoption can falter not because systems lack capability, but because organizations apply employee mental models to systems that do not participate in work as socially embedded employees. This article develops a theoretical model of that mismatch, drawing on theory of mind, psychological contracts, shared mental models, transactive memory, and automation reliance research. It introduces the context discovery gap: a mismatch between the organizational context people assume AI already has or will discover and the context it can actually obtain and use in a workplace. Employee-associated expectations may contribute to this mismatch by leading users to leave relevant background unstated. The article argues that the missing psychology of AI adoption lies in the human assumptions through which AI systems are understood, delegated to, and evaluated. As a conceptual contribution, it connects these assumptions to context provision and reliance, develops testable propositions, and identifies responsibilities for designing and maintaining context discovery.

item.title: Cognitive Load in Generative AI-Supported Learning in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Generative AI is increasingly used in higher education, but how GenAI-supported interaction relates to students’ cognitive load-related experiences remains unclear. This review examined empirical studies published between 2022 and 8 May 2026 that investigated higher education students’ interaction with GenAI systems and cognitive load-related experiences. Twenty-one studies met the inclusion criteria, covering diverse learning contexts including language and writing, STEM, professional education, design, and self-regulated learning. Across studies, findings revealed diverse cognitive patterns rather than a consistent cognitive outcome of GenAI-supported learning. Some studies suggested that GenAI was associated with reduced unnecessary cognitive demands through explanation, feedback, and support. The findings suggest that reduced cognitive demand may reflect effective cognitive support, while some cases may indicate possible cognitive offloading when learners do not actively engage with AI-generated information. Overall, GenAI may provide greater learning value when interaction design reduces unnecessary difficulty while maintaining learners’ active engagement in evaluation and reflection.

item.title: Evaluating AI Alignment in LLMs: Output Analysis of Value Priorities Across 75 Models with Human Benchmarking
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in human-AI interaction research and practice, yet existing capability and safety benchmarks reveal little about the value priorities these systems express or how those priorities correspond to human judgements. Across three studies, we introduce an output-based approach to evaluating one facet of AI alignment by treating LLM-generated text as behavioural data and comparing expressed value-priority profiles with a human reference. Study 1 used inductive qualitative analysis to derive six themes of optimal AI functioning, namely Performance, Adaptive Capacity, Social Good, Ethics and Responsibility, Relational Integration, and Agency. Study 2 showed that LLM outputs were highly stable within models and converged on a common value-priority structure across models, indicating reliable and comparable value profiles. Study 3 benchmarked 75 contemporary LLMs against 376 human respondents using a profile-fidelity metric capturing both the relative ordering of priorities and the calibration of between-priority differences. Although most models reproduced the human ordering of values, some systematically exaggerated the differences between them, showing that models can appear aligned on conventional benchmarks while still diverging from human value calibration. Profile fidelity varied substantially across models and did not consistently scale with size, recency, or capability tier. Both LLMs and humans converged on a deprioritisation of Agency, raising important questions about the development of increasingly agentic AI systems. For research and applied use, the six themes and profile-based metric provide a scalable method for auditing LLM value profiles before deployment in contexts where alignment with human priorities is critical.

item.title: Dancing with REEM-C: A Robot-To-Human Physical-Social Communication Study
item.description:
International Journal of Social Robotics
Humans often work closely together and relay a wealth of information through physical interaction. Robots, on the other hand, are not yet able to work similarly closely with humans and to effectively convey information when engaging in physical-social human-robot interaction (psHRI). This currently limits the potential of human-robot collaboration to solve real-world problems. This paper investigates how to establish clear and intuitive robot-to-human communication, while considering human comfort during psHRI. We approach this question from the perspective of a leader-follower dancing scenario, in which a full-body humanoid robot leads a human by signaling the next steps through a choice of communication modalities including haptic, visual, and audio signals. This is achieved through the development of a split whole-body control framework combining admittance and impedance control on the upper body, with position control on the lower body for balancing and stepping. Robot-led psHRI participant experiments allowed us to verify controller performance, as well as to build an understanding of what types of communication work better from the perspective of human partners, particularly in terms of perceived effectiveness and comfort.

item.title: Research Trends of Artificial Intelligence‐Facilitated Computational Thinking in K‐12 STEM : A Systematic Review Through the Lens of Activity Theory
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), research in the cross‐disciplinary field of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education has increasingly focused on how to leverage AI to foster computational thinking (CT) among K‐12 students, given that CT, recognized as a core 21st‐century competency, plays a pivotal role in cultivating students’ literacy and equipping them with the ability to tackle complex problems. Objective Grounded in activity theory, this study seeks to identify the key factors shaping K‐12 students’ CT development in AI‐enhanced STEM education. It systematically analyzes: (a) the subjects involved and the types and roles of AI tools employed, (b) the purposes, periods, and CT dimensions within the object, (c) the methods, strategies, and evaluation performance applied within rules, (d) the learning domains within communities and the interactions within the division of labor, and (e) the developmental trends in outcomes. Method This study employed the PRISMA framework to systematically review 57 SSCI journal publications published between 2017 and 2025. In addition, Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) was utilized to examine the current state of CT evaluation. Results and Conclusions Findings indicate that: (1) the primary subjects of the studies were elementary school students; expert systems and robotics were the most prevalent types of AI, which were frequently employed as learning tools; (2) the primary objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of AI in CT–K12–STEM, with periods typically ranging from 2 to 6 months, focusing on conceptual knowledge and practical skills; (3) the rules focused on exploratory learning and gamification strategies, employing quantitative research methods; (4) communities spanned cross‐disciplinary domains, with division of labor tending towards mixed interaction types; and (5) outcomes focused on the learning cognitive perspective, encompassing aspects such as learning performance and problem solving. Based on the research results, practical recommendations are provided for educational researchers and policymakers.

item.title: Academic Pressures, Generative AI Use, and Academic Behaviors and Perceptions Among University Students: An Empirical Study
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
This study draws on cognitive offloading theory and self-regulated learning theory to investigate why Chinese university students use Generative AI (GenAI) and what academic correlates are observed. Using a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 500 university students and analyzed through structural equation modeling (SEM) and bootstrap mediation analysis. The results show that academic workload, time pressure, and sensitivity to grades are positively associated with GenAI usage, whereas sensitivity to quality is not. In addition, GenAI usage is positively associated with procrastination and self-reported memory difficulties. Regarding the competing hypotheses on creative engagement, GenAI usage was positively associated with creative engagement, which may indicate that students may use GenAI for ideation rather than answer retrieval. Mediation analyses confirm that GenAI usage significantly mediates the associations between academic workload, time pressure, sensitivity to grades, and the three outcomes. However, the indirect effects of sensitivity to quality on the three outcomes were not significant, consistent with the unsupported hypothesis. The study highlights the need to strengthen students’ AI literacy training, manage academic workload, and redesign assessment methods so as to balance responsible use with academic integrity. Future research should employ longitudinal designs, multi-method measures, and explore these relationships in diverse educational contexts to gain a more comprehensive understanding.

item.title: Students’ intentions to truthfully declare generative AI use in higher education assessment: a cross-sectional SEM study integrating deterrence theory and the theory of planned behavior
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, truthful declaration of GenAI use has become increasingly important for maintaining transparency and supporting the validity and integrity of academic assessment. Drawing on the Theory of Planned behavior (TPB) and deterrence theory, this study examines the psychological factors associated with students’ intentions to truthfully declare their GenAI use. The proposed framework distinguishes between deterrence targeting non-disclosure and deterrence associated with improper GenAI use exposed through truthful declaration. Methods Data were collected through the Credamo platform from currently enrolled university students in China who had experience with GenAI-use declaration in assessed work. A total of 466 valid questionnaires were obtained. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to test the hypothesized relationships, and 5,000 bootstrap resamples were used to estimate confidence intervals for indirect associations. Results Attitude (β = 0.564), subjective norm (β = 0.219), and perceived behavioral control (β = 0.186) were positively associated with truthful declaration intention. Non-disclosure detection certainty (NDC) was positively associated with attitude (β = 0.643) and perceived behavioral control (β = 0.588), whereas improper-use identification certainty (IIC) was negatively associated with both constructs (β = −2.175 and −2.154, respectively). Non-disclosure sanction severity was negatively associated with attitude and perceived behavioral control (β = −0.486 and −0.690, respectively), whereas improper-use sanction severity was positively associated with both constructs (β = 1.916 and 1.892, respectively). All these structural paths were statistically significant ( p < 0.001). Bootstrap analyses identified significant indirect associations with intention via both attitude and perceived behavioral control: positive for non-disclosure detection certainty and improper-use sanction severity, and negative for non-disclosure sanction severity and improper-use identification certainty. Discussion The findings highlight the value of distinguishing deterrence targets and separating detection certainty from sanction severity. These perceptions showed contrasting associations with attitude and perceived behavioral control, with corresponding model-implied indirect associations with truthful declaration intention. The results inform differentiated approaches to disclosure governance, although the conditional sanction-severity estimates require cautious interpretation.

item.title: To cheat or not to cheat? Examining undergraduate students’ use of generative AI and academic dishonesty
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become embedded in everyday university study, intensifying long-standing concerns about academic integrity now that students can obtain finished work on demand. Yet why some students cross the line into academic dishonesty—and whether teaching them to feel capable of and in control of AI protects against it—remains unclear. Framing propensity toward AI-enabled academic dishonesty as the focal educational outcome, and drawing on the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study used an explanatory mixed-methods design. We analyzed a cross-sectional survey of undergraduates across disciplines at several Chinese universities ( N = 1,045 after removing 115 respondents who gave the same answer to all 41 items) and semi-structured interviews with seven students, which were analyzed thematically. Academic dishonesty was common (50.1% of students scored 5 or higher on a 1–7 scale) and was most strongly associated with AI dependence ( β = 0.63), which was in turn associated with impulsivity, trust in AI, and fear of missing out; trust was also directly associated with dishonesty. Contrary to the widely held assumption that agency protects integrity, a sense of human–AI agency did not moderate the dependence–dishonesty association, and was itself positively associated with dishonesty. Habitual verification of AI output showed the complementary pattern: it did not weaken the dependence–dishonesty association, but it was associated with markedly lower dependence, and thus indirectly with less dishonesty. A latent profile analysis converged on the same account—dependence ordered the profiles on dishonesty, whereas felt agency did not order them at all—and interviewees invoked a sense of control when accounting for passing AI work off as their own. Because the survey was cross-sectional and self-reported, these are associations, not demonstrated effects. For teaching and integrity policy, they nonetheless suggest that curbing dependence and calibrating students’ trust in AI, rather than cultivating a general sense of agency, are the more promising targets.

item.title: Temporal dissociation across the eye-brain-muscle cascade delineates a preparation window before muscle activation in subacute stroke
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Upper-limb motor impairment after stroke is compounded by a disrupted sensorimotor cascade linking visual attention, cortical motor preparation, and peripheral muscle activation. Whether these stages are temporally dissociated in subacute stroke, and whether their timing carries information about the preparation and execution of a reaching action, remains unclear. Thirty subacute stroke survivors and 30 healthy controls performed a full-plane nine-grid reaching task while eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and surface electromyography (EMG) were recorded synchronously. Three neurophysiological latencies were extracted: first fixation on the target, stimulus-locked lateralized readiness potential (s-LRP) onset, and peripheral muscle activation onset. Compared with controls, patients showed a stepwise delay across the cascade, with delayed visual engagement (616.73 ms vs. 367.86 ms) and delayed peripheral muscle activation (1,080 ms vs. 605 ms) bracketing a cortical preparation window. A random-forest classifier was trained on window-level gaze-timing features, computed separately for each target-presentation and inter-target interval of the task. Under participant-level leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, it achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.973 (95% CI 0.958–0.984) and an accuracy of 0.918, numerically the highest among the five classifiers compared. These findings describe a quantifiable temporal organization of the sensorimotor cascade in the subacute stage of stroke and indicate that gaze timing carries discriminative information about the occurrence of an instructed reaching action. They establish a descriptive, testable framework rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit. Validation in chronic stroke and across independent samples is further required.

item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers
item.description:
Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: The impact of an AI ‐driven multimodal teaching analytics dashboard on pre‐service teachers' reflective learning in microteaching
item.description:
British Journal of Educational Technology
Abstract Microteaching is a cornerstone of teacher education, enabling pre‐service teachers (PSTs) to rehearse, observe and refine instructional practices through structured reflection. Traditional video‐based review in microteaching is often time‐consuming and insufficiently analytical. Although learning analytics dashboards (LADs) can visualize teaching data to support reflection, many remain descriptive, offering limited insight into how behavioural evidence relates to pedagogical meaning. To address this gap, this study introduces iTeachBoard, an AI‐driven multimodal teaching analytics dashboard that integrates layered multimodal timeline visualization based on data‐storytelling design principle with LLM‐generated narrative feedback to support reflective learning in microteaching. A quasi‐experimental study ( n = 53) compared iTeachBoard with a conventional visual analytics dashboard (VAD). Results revealed that iTeachBoard significantly enhanced PSTs' data interpretation, meaning construction and reflective writing depth. Participants perceived narrative‐style feedback as more trustworthy, explainable and pedagogically relevant. These findings suggest that LLM‐driven multimodal learning analytics can help bridge data visualization and pedagogical interpretation, thereby supporting PSTs' sense‐making, particularly data interpretation and meaning construction, as well as reflective writing depth in microteaching. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Microteaching offers pre‐service teachers (PSTs) valuable opportunities to rehearse lessons, receive feedback and reflect on their teaching. However, reflections often remain superficial due to limited feedback structure and lack of actionable guidance. Learning analytics dashboards (LADs) can visualize teaching behaviours, but most rely on descriptive metrics that lack interpretability and pedagogical relevance. Sense‐making and data‐storytelling design principles have been proposed to help PSTs connect learning data with pedagogical meaning, yet empirical validation in teacher education remains scarce. What this paper adds Introduces iTeachBoard, an AI‐driven multimodal LAD that integrates large language model (LLM)‐based narrative feedback with multimodal visualizations to support deep reflective learning in microteaching. Proposes the AI for Microteaching Multimodal Analytics Model (AI4MT), linking observable teaching behaviours to pedagogically meaningful reflective dimensions. Provides empirical evidence that narrative‐style feedback combined with multimodal visualization significantly improves PSTs' overall sense‐making, with significant gains in data interpretation and meaning construction, as well as reflective writing depth, compared with a conventional video analytics dashboard. Implications for practice and/or policy iTeachBoard can be implemented in teacher education and professional development to promote evidence‐based reflection, collaborative lesson analysis and continuous pedagogical improvement. The dashboard can enhance teachers' data literacy and AI literacy, fostering meaningful engagement with multimodal feedback for reflective growth. Institutions should develop policies ensuring ethical data use, privacy protection and transparency in AI‐supported reflective systems to promote responsible adoption in educational settings.

item.title: Beyond access: guided versus free ChatGPT use and learning outcomes in higher education
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
Research on artificial intelligence in higher education has largely examined usage patterns rather than the cognitive dimensions of student-AI interaction. This mixed-methods experimental study investigated how undergraduates’ epistemic engagement with ChatGPT during academic reasoning tasks relates to learning outcomes. Grounded in constructivist learning theory, the study randomly assigned 120 undergraduates to three conditions: No-AI control, Free-AI (unstructured access), and Guided-AI (process-focused scaffolding). Students completed epistemic reasoning tasks requiring conceptual understanding and judgment under ambiguity. Analysis identified four interaction profiles: Delegative (AI-led), Instrumental (procedural), Co-Constructive (shared control), and Dialogic-Critical (student-led critique). Task quality varied by interaction pattern rather than AI access alone; Delegative users showed no measurable advantage over No-AI controls despite having AI access. A minimal intervention, a single-page handout emphasizing questioning strategies, substantially increased dialogic engagement (d = 2.29) and critical evaluation (d = 2.19). Because profiles were observed rather than assigned, profile-outcome relationships are reported as associations. Findings challenge binary debates over AI prohibition versus permission, indicating that educational value is associated with students’ epistemic stance during interaction. Pedagogical scaffolding, rather than surveillance or restriction, may be the most productive institutional response to generative AI.

item.title: Critical yet dependent? Time poverty, critical AI engagement, and generative AI dependence in university interactive learning environments
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
Generative AI has become an interactive learning resource, yet repeated delegation to AI may also coincide with difficulty working without it. This cross-sectional questionnaire study examined theory-consistent covariance patterns among time poverty, AI self-efficacy, perceived social support, AI critical thinking, effort enjoyment belief (EEB), and generative AI dependence in 1,862 first-year students from three higher-education institutions in Northwest China. Time poverty and AI critical thinking were positively associated with dependence, while AI self-efficacy and PSS were positively associated with AI critical thinking. In the primary specification, EEB moderated the time poverty-AI critical thinking and AI critical thinking-dependence associations, although both interactions were small. The findings distinguish critical engagement with AI from reported reliance and highlight time pressure as a potentially important feature of students’ AI use.

item.title: Impacts of AI ‐Generated Learning Videos on Learning Outcomes: The Mediating Roles of Perceived Desirability and Perceived Feasibility
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background In recent educational research and practice, there has been growing attention to the use and impact of generative AI technologies, with most studies focusing on AI‐generated textual content. However, relatively little is known about AI‐generated learning videos, despite their potential to significantly influence learners' experiences and outcomes. Objectives Drawing on situational interest theory and construal level theory, this study investigates how three different types of AI‐generated learning videos influence learning outcomes through the mediating roles of perceived desirability and perceived feasibility. Three AI‐generated video types that represent ascending levels of learner involvement—situated videos, multiple‐choice interactive situated videos, and AI–learner co‐created videos—are examined. Methods A between‐subjects experiment was conducted with 221 valid responses across four conditions: three AI‐generated learning video types and a traditional learning video control condition. ANOVA and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM) were employed to validate the effects. Results and Conclusions Results show that all three types of AI‐generated videos significantly enhance learning outcomes—learning enjoyment, learning performance, and continuous learning intention—compared to traditional learning videos, with perceived feasibility mediating the effects on all three outcomes and perceived desirability mediating the effects on learning enjoyment and continuous learning intention. This study extends the theoretical boundaries of AI in learning research and provides actionable insights for teachers in instructional design.

item.title: Student Responses to Cognitive Conflicts in GenAI ‐Assisted Learning: A Covariate‐Dependent Markov Chain Analysis on Human‐ AI Interactions
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reshapes the learning process, students will inevitably experience cognitive conflicts when their existing knowledge and beliefs clash with information provided by GenAI. Improper handling of cognitive conflicts may lead to a decline in students' learning efficiency and even hinder the development of critical thinking skills. Objective This study aims to understand how students respond to cognitive conflicts during their interactions with GenAI, with a focus on comparing high‐performing and low‐performing student groups. Methods To identify relationships between cognitive conflict intensity and students' responses, we used a covariate‐dependent Markov chain (a sequential data modelling method) to analyse the response states of 411 students in a simulated academic writing task and observed transitions in student response states across different task performances. Results The results revealed that the intensity of cognitive conflict had a significant impact on students' state transitions. Overall, as the level of conflict increased, students' state changes exhibited a phased pattern, shifting from fluctuation (transitioning to a variety of different states) to inertia or convergence (maintaining the original state or transitioning uniformly to a negative response state). Student response state transitions varied across different task performance levels. Conclusions This study provides a novel methodological perspective for modelling sequential response dynamics in Human‐AI interaction. The findings offer new insights into the cognitive conflict dynamics in GenAI‐assisted learning, providing implications for designing GenAI‐assisted learning environments.

item.title: Same Stimulus, Different Ideas: Prior Knowledge and the Integration of AI-Generated Stimuli in Creative Ideation
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
External stimuli can expand the conceptual space during creative ideation, yet individuals may incorporate the same stimuli differently depending on the knowledge and experience available to them. This issue bears on the information-processing mechanisms of creativity and on the use of generative artificial intelligence as a source of stimuli. Nine groups (221 participants) from three educational and sociocultural contexts (Indigenous and Afro-descendant community members holding traditional knowledge, rural school students, and university students) took part in ideation workshops to design agro-industrial products. Stimuli were generated with a large language model. Semantic and conceptual embedding similarity and topic modelling were used to compare initial ideas, stimuli, and final ideas. Topic models of these very short texts were unstable. In the community and school groups, conceptual integration generally stayed close to the initial proximity between ideas and stimuli, whereas the university groups more often exceeded it, a tendency that held across alternative representations but not in every group. Coffee-domain groups, whose ideas and stimuli shared the vocabulary of the raw material, combined high persistence with high integration. Three exploratory forms of integration are proposed: conceptual reinterpretation, expansion, and transformation. The analyses are descriptive, and prior knowledge was not measured directly.

item.title: Cognitive Predictors of AI-Related Textual Change in Upper-Intermediate L2 Russian Writing: Working Memory, Attention Control, and Critical Thinking
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can alter final second-language (L2) texts, yet cognitive differences may shape which changes emerge. This exploratory study examined 38 upper-intermediate learners of Russian who each produced one composition with AI assistance and one without it. Working memory, attention control, and critical thinking were measured continuously, and 11 textual outcomes were calculated from paired compositions. AI-assisted texts showed higher lemma-based lexical-diversity values, longer words, more connectives per 100 words, and substantially fewer first-person markers, while total word count, sentence measures, and formulaic-expression rate did not differ in the full sample. The higher POS-based content-word density was attenuated after first-person forms were excluded, suggesting a contribution from the change in person marking. Exploratory models suggested negative working-memory associations with lexical-diversity and connective-rate change, and negative attention-control associations with lexical-diversity change. The positive working-memory coefficient for word-count change was sensitive to HC3 estimation and leave-one-out refitting. Critical thinking showed no clear independent association in the primary change-score models, while positive coefficients for MATTR and HD-D appeared in the outcome-conditioned models. Under this supervised, student-mediated procedure, AI assistance was associated with lexical, discourse-marking, and stance differences in completed L2 texts.

item.title: Generative AI use and self-perceived employability among young adults in China: indirect associations through career decision-making self-efficacy and trust in generative AI
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into university students’ learning and career preparation, its relationship with perceived employment prospects warrants closer examination. This study investigated the association between GenAI use and self-perceived employability, with career decision-making self-efficacy and trust in GenAI specified as parallel mediators. Methods Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 579 university students in China. Structural equation modeling and bias-corrected bootstrap analyses with 5,000 resamples were used to examine the proposed relationships while controlling for gender, age, educational background, and work experience. Results GenAI use was positively associated with self-perceived employability, and both career decision-making self-efficacy and trust in GenAI showed significant indirect associations. The direct association remained significant after including both mediators, indicating partial statistical mediation. Discussion These findings identify two complementary psychological pathways involving confidence in personal career decision-making capabilities and trust in technological resources, contributing to understanding the psychological dimensions of GenAI engagement in university students’ career preparation. Practically, the findings suggest exploring GenAI-supported career education alongside independent decision-making and critical evaluation of generated advice. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal conclusions, and self-perceived employability should be distinguished from demonstrated competence and actual employment outcomes. Longitudinal and experimental research is needed to assess these relationships over time.

item.title: When a feature becomes a bug: evolutionary mismatch in human–robot interaction
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As robots become increasingly integrated into everyday life, evolved psychological mechanisms originally adapted for human social interaction may shape responses to artificial agents in ways that are no longer functionally appropriate. Drawing on an evolutionary psychology framework, the present study examined how anthropomorphism, empathy, and systemizing influence decisions involving a humanoid home robot. Participants ( N = 519) completed an online experiment in which they viewed one of six robot stimuli varying in appearance (human-like, ambiguous, or robotic) and gender (female or male). They then read a scenario in which the manufacturer instructed them to reset the malfunctioning robot, thereby erasing its memories, while the robot pleaded not to be deactivated. Participants rated their willingness to deactivate the robot and the anticipated discomfort associated with doing so, and subsequently completed measures of anthropomorphism, empathy, and systemizing. Two 2 × 3 general linear models showed that stronger anthropomorphic tendencies predicted lower willingness to deactivate the robot, whereas higher systemizing predicted greater willingness. Empathy did not predict the decision itself but was associated with greater anticipated discomfort, together with anthropomorphism, while systemizing predicted lower discomfort. Contrary to our expectations, the decision to deactivate the robot did not vary as a function of its appearance. However, robot appearance influenced anticipated discomfort through interaction effects. These findings suggest that distinct evolved psychological mechanisms differentially shape behavioral and emotional responses to humanoid robots, consistent with the notion that evolutionary mismatch is at play human–robot interactions.

item.title: The dark side of GenAI in the workplace: technostress, loneliness, and the buffering role of transformational leadership
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the workplace, but it also introduces technostress that affects employees’ psychological states and behavioral consequences. However, existing research has yet to offer an integrated framework that explicates the socio-emotional processes and work outcomes of GenAI integration, along with the boundary conditions that moderate these relationships. To bridge this gap, this study integrates the Stressor-Strain-Outcome (SSO) framework and the Conservation of Resources (COR) theory to examine how GenAI-induced technostress influences work loneliness and work effort. Using survey data from 290 public school teachers in Taiwan, this study finds that GenAI-induced technostress is negatively associated with work effort indirectly through work loneliness, whereas its direct effect is not statistically significant. Moreover, transformational leadership weakens the negative relationship between work loneliness and work effort; however, it does not significantly moderate the GenAI-induced technostress-work loneliness link nor the overall moderated mediation effect. This study contributes to the literature by proposing a technostress-work loneliness-work effort pathway from a resource depletion perspective, and by elucidating the boundary conditions under which transformational leadership, as a critical resource buffer, functions in this mechanism in the context of GenAI-driven work environments. From a practical standpoint, these findings offer actionable insights for organizations seeking to foster sustainable GenAI integration while safeguarding employee well-being.

item.title: Learning with GenAI across campuses: student experiences of GenAI-enhanced cybersecurity education
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet limited research has examined how GenAI-supported learning operates alongside geographically distributed peer collaboration. This qualitative study explores student experiences in an AI-enhanced cross-campus cybersecurity learning environment connecting university campuses in California, United States, and Ontario, Canada. Anonymous reflections were collected from 19 students (nine in California and ten in Ontario) about their experiences with GenAI-supported learning, cross-campus interaction, associated challenges, and recommendations for improving the learning experience. The findings indicate that students perceived GenAI as supporting concept clarification, greater perceived learning efficiency, idea development, and problem-solving, while also emphasizing the importance of critically evaluating GenAI-generated information. Cross-campus interaction was perceived as exposing students to diverse perspectives, experiences, and approaches to cybersecurity, which participants described as broadening their understanding of collaborative problem-solving across contexts. Students nevertheless identified challenges involving scheduling, technology, differences in experience, GenAI accuracy, and responsible use. They recommended more structured cross-campus projects, hands-on activities, clearer guidance on ethical GenAI use, and greater engagement with industry professionals. The study contributes to research on technology-enhanced learning in higher education by suggesting how GenAI-supported learning and geographically distributed peer interaction can provide complementary educational resources: GenAI offers immediate cognitive and informational support, while cross-campus interaction provides access to situated human perspectives. Together, these experiences highlight the importance of verification, contextual judgment, critical AI literacy, and intentional pedagogical design in GenAI-enhanced learning environments.

item.title: Digital meditation at scale: a randomized citizen science trial comparing four meditation practices
item.description:
BMC Psychology
This preregistered randomized controlled trial evaluated whether app-delivered meditation improved psychological, cognitive, and physiological outcomes relative to an active control, whether four meditation techniques differed in their effects, and whether individual differences moderated response. A total of 1,211 adults were randomized to four weeks of app-guided loving-kindness, mantra, body scan, or nondual meditation, or to a classical-music active control. Self-report (well-being, mood, self-transcendence, nondual awareness, interoception, compassion), cognitive (Stroop, N-back), and physiological (electroencephalography (EEG), heart rate variability (HRV), heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEP)) outcomes were assessed before and after the intervention and analyzed with linear mixed models and false-discovery-rate correction. No preregistered meditation-versus-control outcome survived FDR correction, and Bayes factors additionally favored the null for the temporal EEG measures. None of the four preregistered technique-specific hypotheses was supported. Two self-report outcomes showed arm differences surviving correction on non-predicted contrasts (self-compassion isolation and sleep quality, both q = 0.050), and mantra participants showed faster working-memory reaction time than body scan participants. The four techniques did not differ from one another. In exploratory moderation analyses, trait neuroticism moderated the meditation effect on working-memory reaction time, with higher-neuroticism participants showing greater benefit in cognitive speed than controls. Four weeks of app-based meditation was not superior to an active music control across psychological, cognitive, and physiological measures, and no preregistered technique-specific hypothesis was supported. The neuroticism finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants replication. Endpoint data were available for 43% of randomized participants and missingness was non-random, which limits inference. This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/xdjfq/overview) on October 24, 2024. International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number, ISRCTN10867561, retrospectively registered on August​ 12, 2026.

item.title: Making sense of generative AI: a comparative study of students’ appropriation of generative AI in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Germany
item.description:
Learning Media and Technology
Over the past few years, university students around the world have rapidly incorporated generative AI applications into their academic practices. While research has begun to examine students’ patterns of use, perceived benefits and risks, and institutional responses, little is known about how students in different higher education contexts practically appropriate and make sense of generative AI as part of their studies. Taking a practice-theoretical position, this study posits that the adoption of generative AI as an epistemic rather than an educational technology can only be understood in relation to existing practices and their associated epistemic regimes. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 29 students in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Germany, this study explores the complex ways students engage with generative AI in different educational settings. The findings reveal a predominantly instrumental stance on generative AI across all settings. It is argued that this stance enables students to stay in control of the epistemic activities while simultaneously making them susceptible to rote computing and mechanical processing. This study contributes to critical research on learning, media, and technology by rendering salient students’ situated entanglements with emerging technologies and prevalent epistemic regimes.

item.title: Questioning practices in AI-mediated academic writing: a case study of final-year undergraduates using ChatGPT
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
This interpretive qualitative case study examines how final-year undergraduates construct and rationalise questions when using ChatGPT for academic writing. Data comprised 20 participant-specific ChatGPT logs containing approximately 65,000 words and 338 questions, alongside interviews with the same 20 Malaysian students. Questions underwent deductive qualitative content analysis integrating Revised Bloom's Taxonomy and adapted Socratic Questioning categories. Interviews were analysed inductively, and emergent themes were compared with log patterns. Students primarily used ChatGPT to clarify concepts, connect theories and sources to their research, and verify writing decisions. Clarification and probing for evidence accounted for 83.4% of questions, while testing assumptions represented only 0.9%. Although Evaluating and Creating questions occurred, interviews indicated motivations centred on reassurance, academic compliance, and error avoidance rather than sustained intellectual challenge. These findings reveal a disconnection between cognitive complexity and epistemic challenge: cognitively advanced questions can remain epistemically conservative when seeking confirmation without examining evidence, premises, or alternatives. We conceptualise this pattern as epistemic minimalism: sophisticated prompting that advances text production without proportionate scrutiny of AI-generated knowledge. Integrating cognitive level with dialogic function distinguishes questions that stabilise AI outputs from those that make them contestable, reframing GenAI literacy as responsibility for interrogating evidence, assumptions, and scholarly judgement.

item.title: Value of a Human Mind: How Perceived AI-Authorship Shapes Willingness to Pay for Cultural Goods
item.description:
Creativity Research Journal
Artificial intelligence is increasingly involved in the production of cultural goods, raising important questions about how consumers evaluate creativity. This research examines how perceived authorship, whether a work is believed to be created by a human or by artificial intelligence, shapes willingness to pay. Across five experiments, we manipulate the attributed origin of artworks while holding the visual stimulus constant, isolating the psychological consequences of authorship beliefs rather than objective production differences. Results reveal a robust preference for works believed to be human-created. This effect is driven primarily by lower perceived authenticity and emotional sensitivity attributed to AI creators. Egocentrism further moderates the relationship, such that consumers lower in egocentrism exhibit stronger preferences for human authorship. Two predicted boundary conditions, the expressive purpose of the artwork and framing AI as a creative tool, did not significantly alter the effect, suggesting that the perceived presence of a human mind serves as a powerful signal in consumer valuation. These findings advance current understanding of how perceived authorship influences the value of cultural goods and contribute to broader theories of creativity by highlighting the enduring psychological importance of human agency in artistic contexts. Practical implications extend to creators, marketers, and platforms, navigating the integration of AI into cultural production.
